entries.title: Michigan rolls over Arizona in Final Four, will play UConn for national title
entries.summary: <p>INDIANAPOLIS — Michigan overpowered Arizona early and humbled the ’Cats all night long, turning the Final Four meeting billed as the Game of the Year into a 91-73 Wolverines highlight reel Saturday night.</p><p>Junior center Aday Mara scored a career-high 26 points and had nine rebounds, a dinged-up Yaxel Lendeborg had 11 points in 14 minutes and the Blue blew through their fifth straight March Madness opponent by double digits while becoming the first team to break 90 points five times in a single tournament.</p><p>Next up, a title matchup Monday against UConn, a 71-62 winner over Illinois in the early semifinal that was billed — wrongly — as the undercard to this battle of No. 1 seeds.</p><p>Michigan and Arizona came in with the nation’s top two defenses, a pair of top-five offenses and somewhere between eight and a dozen NBA stars between them.</p><p>But it was the Wolverines (36-3) who looked like pros, running to a double-digit lead only 5:31 into the contest, then swatting and slamming Arizona into oblivion.</p><p>Koa Peat had a quiet 16 points and 11 rebounds for the Big 12 champion Wildcats (36-3). They shot 6 for 17 from 3, 36% overall and had two assists and nine turnovers over a first half that ended with them trailing 48-32. Sparkplug Jaden Bradley got his fourth foul 94 seconds into the second half and finished with 13 points, most in extended garbage time.</p>
entries.author: AP

entries.title: Boy, 15, wounded in Bronzeville shooting
entries.summary: <p>A 15-year-old boy was wounded in a shooting Saturday night in Bronzeville on the South Side. </p><p>The boy was outside in the 300 block of East 43rd Street around 7:20 p.m. when he was struck in the right arm by gunfire, Chicago police said. </p><p>He was taken to Comer Children's Hospital where he was listed in good condition, police said. </p><p>Area 1 detectives were investigating. </p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Philip Zinckernagel, Chris Brady help Fire hand Nashville first loss of season
entries.summary: <p>Philip Zinckernagel scored 17 seconds into the match and Chris Brady made it stand up as the Fire handed Nashville SC its first loss this season with a 1-0 victory on Saturday night at Soldier Field.</p><p>The Fire (3-2-1) stunned Nashville (4-1-1) when Zinckernagel used passes from Jonathan Bamba and Anton Salétros to score for the first time this season. It was the earliest goal ever scored by the Fire and the 10th fastest in league history.</p><p>Zinckernagel had 15 goals and 15 assists last season, his first in the league. Bamba's assist was his first after collecting 10 as a newcomer last year. Salétros earned his first in first season in the league.</p><p>Brady saved four shots for Chicago. He has posted three clean sheets and surrendered just five goals in six starts this season. It was Brady's 23rd shutout in 98 career starts — all with the Fire.</p><p>Rookie Brian Schwake had two saves for Nashville. He allowed two goals and had three clean sheets in his first five starts.</p><p>Hugo Cuypers had a run of four straight matches with a goal come to an end for Chicago, which began a stretch of playing five of six matches at Soldier Field.</p><p>Nashville swept the Fire last season and had won four in a row in the series — three by shutouts. Nashville leads the series 6-2-2.</p><p><b>Up next</b></p><p>Nashville: Visits Charlotte FC on Saturday.</p><p>Chicago: Hosts Atlanta United on Saturday.<br></p>
entries.author: AP

entries.title: Illini fans in Chicago lament Final Four loss, but leave season with 'something to be excited about'
entries.summary: <p>The noise at Mullen’s Sports Bar and Grill in West Ridge came in waves with every dunk, missed shot and defensive miscue during the University of Illinois' Final Four matchup against the University of Connecticut. </p><p>"It's unifying," said Kayla Mendoza, who was watching alongside her sister and mother, a U. of I. alumna, at the bar Saturday night. "We're really coming together now." </p><p>It didn't all come together for the Illini, whose <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/college-sports/2026/04/04/uconn-beats-illinois-ncaa-final-four-dan-hurley-braylon-mullins-keaton-wagler-arizona-michigan" >second-half rally fell short 71-62</a> to keep fans waiting at least another year for the flagship state school's first national championship. But for dozens of orange- and navy-clad patrons who packed the bar for the game, the future still looked bright. </p><p>And it sure didn't hurt business at Mullen's, uniting fans and regulars alike as the team made its biggest run in two decades. </p><p>"It's a different crowd than it is for an NCAA game," said Mullen's manager Carrie Maw said. "A lot more alumni come in... Lively people come in, they have a great time." </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" halftime, fans were stressed but still optimistic as the Illini trailed 37-29.</p><p>"Our defense is not defending. We're not guarding. We need to get stops," a frustrated Mendoza said. "I don't know what's happening." </p><p>Skokie resident and lifelong fan Deb Shawver, 56 — dressed in her alumnus father's old button-down Illini shirt — had her eyes glues to the screen. She marveled at the pressure facing youngsters in the nationally televised game. </p><p>"It's crazy because these kids are like pro athletes," Shawver said. "The pressure's on them when they're like 18, 19, 20 years old." </p><p>As the Illini trailed late in the first half, Shawver kept her confidence. "I think their nerves are calm and they're getting back in there." </p><p>The crowd gradually grew louder as the Illini cut the deficit to six points with seven minutes left in the game. Chants of "I-L-L" broke out as the team looked to shift momentum.</p><p>“We have to get the f------ rebounds,” an even more frustrated Mendoza said as the game entered its final minutes. “I’m hopeful, I’m fired up.”</p><p>Some fans stood from their seats in anticipation as the Illini trailed by five with under three minutes to go. Within seconds, fans collectively groaned and cheered as UConn and Illinois traded three-pointers. </p><p>“Let’s do the math,” one patron said as he tried to calculate how the Illini could erase a two-possession deficit with under a minute left.</p><p>But as the numbers fell out of favor and the seconds ticked down on Illinois' season, Karina Mendoza — Kayla's sister — looked on with dejection. “I didn’t see the desire to continue fighting," she said. “Connecticut deserved it, honestly. entries.title: UConn beats cold-shooting Illinois 71-62, ending Illini's NCAA run in national semifinal
entries.summary: <p>INDIANAPOLIS — The tears flowed.</p><p>They always do when the end of something this good, this worthwhile, comes too damn soon.</p><p>Alas, not this year.</p><p>Not this <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/college-sports" target="_blank" >Illini</a> team.</p><p>Someday, perhaps soon, Illinois will break through with its first men’s basketball national championship. Thirty-six Illini teams have gotten to the NCAA Tournament, winning a total of 50 games — second-most among schools that haven’t won the whole thing — but each endeavor has ended short of the mountaintop.</p><p>This one ended Saturday in a national semifinal against UConn, which turned out to be a cut above Illinois after all and won 71-62.</p><p>The Huskies (34-5) might not have better players than the Illini (28-9), but they rose to the occasion as though it were a matter of fact. Superstar coach Dan Hurley might not have better X’s and O’s scribbled on his whiteboard, but for stretches it looked like the Huskies knew a few things the Illini didn’t.</p><p>The fact Illinois' two lowest-scoring, worst-shooting games this season were against UConn — it was 74-61 Huskies the day after Thanksgiving — should give coach Underwood something to think about and wrestle with after the first Final Four appearance of his career.</p><p>But that can wait a bit.</p><p>“I feel sad,” coach Brad Underwood said, his voice catching. “I’m sad. If you want to know the truth, I’m sad.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/college-sports/2026/04/03/illinois-uconn-final-four-illini-huskies-underwood-hurley-have-fun-spill-guts-no-regrets" >Illinois’ Final Four marching orders: Have fun, spill guts, no regrets</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/college-sports/2026/03/29/illinois-michigan-big-ten-final-four-championship-drought-michigan-state-spartans-mateen-cleaves-tom-izzo-2000" >Illinois, Michigan give Big Ten two shots at ending quarter-century-long title drought. Is this the year?</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/college-sports/2026/03/29/illinois-uconn-final-four-illini-huskies-mullins-hurley-underwood-arizona-michigan-march-madness-indianapolis" target="_blank" >Illinois will face UConn in Final Four in rematch of Huskies’ November victory</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>While the Illini bricked one three-point attempt after another — they finished 6-for-26 — the Huskies made enough of their own to outscore the Illini by 18 from behind the arc, a crucial area in which the guys in orange failed to deliver.</p><p>There were missed long shots that looked on target, missed short shots that confounded the Illini by not rolling in. Missed shots of all kinds, really, for a team that has been proud of its top offensive efficiency rating all season yet laid a 33.9% egg from the field on the biggest stage in college basketball.</p><p>“I’ve never seen that before,” senior Kylan Boswell said, wiping his eyes at his locker. “I’ve never personally shot layups and they’ve bounced in and out like how they did today. [Expletive] just happens. You can’t make excuses at the end of the day.”</p><p>“Maybe it’s the uniforms,” Underwood offered. “We make those shots against everybody else.”</p><p>Or maybe UConn — which bills itself as the “Basketball Capital of the World” — just has the secret sauce. Six national titles for the Huskies men, all in the last 26 tournaments, and an amazing record in Final Four games of 13-1. A win against Arizona or Michigan on Monday would mean a third title in four years for Hurley’s program. And that’s not even mentioning the UConn women, who’ve cut down the nets 12 times.</p><p>There were moments in this game when the Illini appeared to be squarely in the fight. One came in the first half, when a Tomislav Ivisic three gave them their first lead at 22-21. Andrej Stojakovic then went to the line with a chance to widen the edge, but he missed both free throws. The Huskies then ripped off a 13-2 run and led 37-29 at the half.</p><p>Less than four minutes into the second half, Ivisic missed a wide-open three that could’ve made it a five-point game, gotten the pro-Illini crowd on its feet and put real pressure on the Huskies. But the shot rimmed out and, seven seconds later, UConn’s Solo Ball stepped into one at the other end and drained it to make it 47-36.</p><p>Later, a Stojakovic layup attempt somehow didn’t go in, the ball coming almost to a complete stop on the back of the rim before finally spinning off. But another Ball three bounded off the rim, soared halfway to the Lucas Oil Stadium ceiling and somehow dropped in, making it 52-40.</p><p>It was that kind of a night.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">all the bounces <a href="https://t.co/kBMfJTrZwP">pic.twitter.com/kBMfJTrZwP</a></p>— UConn Men's Basketball (@UConnMBB) <a href="https://twitter.com/UConnMBB/status/2040575905412633053?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">April 4, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.twitter.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>The Illini made it close during the last several minutes, cutting the deficit to four points twice, but they never had a shot at a tie or the lead. And if they’d had such a chance, on this night? It probably wouldn’t have worked out.</p><p>In what likely was his last college game, Keaton Wagler led the Illini with 20 points. Ivisic scored 16. UConn got 17 from Tarris Reed Jr. and four three-pointers from Indianapolis-area native Braylon Mullins.</p><p>“I feel like the season went by super fast,” Wagler said. “I didn’t want to end at all, but I’m just super glad that it happened and blessed to be a part of this team.”</p><p>At that, the freshman, an expected NBA lottery pick, hung his head and buried his face in a towel, teammate Ty Rodgers’ arm gently around his neck and shoulders.</p><p>“Yeah,” Wagler said after a lengthy pause, “just blessed to be a part of it.”</p><p>After the loss, Underwood told his team how proud he was and how much he loved them. He promised them they would win in life and thanked them for making history.</p><p>Illinois’ first Final Four run in 21 years was well worth the ride.</p><p>Whether or not it went as far as it could will be up for debate forever.</p>
